summary: Defines a basic set of managed objects for SNMP management of extended QoS features of cable modems and cable modem termination systems that follow DOCSIS versions 1.1 and 2.0. It is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: A control panel for checking and adjusting how cable internet connections share speed fairly.

subtitle: The SNMP objects for watching how cable modems and head-end gear split bandwidth into quality-of-service flows.

tldr.problem: DOCSIS 1.1 and 2.0 cable networks give each subscriber's traffic its own quality-of-service treatment, but operators had no standard SNMP objects to see which flows, classifiers and parameters were in effect.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines the DOCS-IETF-QOS-MIB module, organized as 11 tables, that report service flows, packet classifiers, QoS parameter sets, statistics and logs on cable modems (CMs) and cable modem termination systems (CMTSs).
tldr.outcome: Operators and billing tools get a standard read view of DOCSIS QoS, plus a small set of writable tables for named service classes and external classification. The RFC was later updated by RFC 9141.

today: RFC 4323 is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 9141. The module was registered under { mib-2 127 } in the SMI Numbers registry.

sections.title: What the MIB Is For
sections.content:
RFC 4323 is a product of the IP over Cable Data Network (IPCDN) working group. It defines a MIB module, a set of managed objects read over SNMP, for the extended quality-of-service (QoS) features of Cable Modems and Cable Modem Termination Systems that follow the DOCSIS specifications versions 1.1 and 2.0.

The module is derived from the DOCSIS 2.0 Radio Frequency Interface specification. The RFC points out that those specifications only require cable modems to process IPv4 customer traffic, and the MIB's design choices reflect that. It adds that future versions of DOCSIS are expected to require IPv6 support as well.

The module is written in SMIv2 and uses the RFC 2119 requirement words. See RFC 2578, RFC 2579 and RFC 2580 for the SMIv2 rules and RFC 3410 for the management framework.
sections.eli5: It is a list of dials and meters that a cable company can read to see how each customer's internet traffic is being treated.

sections.title: Key DOCSIS Terms
sections.content:
The RFC opens with a glossary. The ones you need most:

  • CM is the cable modem. It bridges the subscriber's LAN onto the cable television radio frequency (RF) network.
  • CMTS is the head-end device that connects the RF network to the Internet.
  • Service Flow (SF) is a unidirectional stream of packets between the CM and the CMTS, either upstream or downstream. It is the fundamental unit of service on a DOCSIS network. The CMTS gives each one a 32-bit SFID. An upstream flow with a non-empty active parameter set also gets a 16-bit SID.
  • Primary SF: every CM has a primary upstream and a primary downstream flow, which carry packets not classified to any other flow.
  • Service Class Name (SCN) is a named set of QoS parameters used as the default values for flows that belong to that class.
  • PHS (Payload Header Suppression) replaces header bytes that repeat across a flow's packets with a one-byte index.
  • DSA, DSC and DSD are the Dynamic Service Addition, Change and Delete MAC messages. DSA and DSC are three-message exchanges (request, response, acknowledgment). DSD is a two-message exchange.
sections.eli5: A service flow is like a lane on a road, going one way only. Each lane has its own speed rules, and a named class is a ready-made set of rules you can give to a lane.

sections.title: Service Flows and QoS Parameter Sets
sections.content:
A service flow is associated with three QoS Parameter Sets (QPSs), nested like boxes. The Provisioned set is the maximum service envelope the flow is authorized for. The Admitted set is what the flow has asked the RF network to reserve but is not yet using. The Active set is what the flow is actually using.

The admitted set exists for cases like IP telephony. During a voice call the far end may ring for up to four minutes, so bandwidth can be reserved without being consumed in the meantime. An inner set is within an outer one when it demands equal or fewer network resources.

A QPS is also an attribute of a Service Class. A configuration file or DSA message can create a flow by giving only a Service Class Name, and the CMTS then copies that class's parameters into the flow's sets, which the RFC calls expanding the macro. Later changes to the class do not affect flows already expanded from it.
sections.eli5: Think of a movie ticket. The provisioned set is the most you are allowed to do, the admitted set is the seat saved for you, and the active set is what you are doing right now.

sections.title: The Eleven Tables
sections.content:
The module is organized as 11 tables under docsIetfQosMIBObjects, registered as { mib-2 127 }. Most tables exist on both the CM and the CMTS. The upstream statistics table and the service flow log table exist on the CMTS only.

  • docsIetfQosPktClassTable: the service flow classifiers in use. Read-only, because classifiers can only be created by a CM configuration file or DSA messages.
  • docsIetfQosParamSetTable: the active, admitted and provisioned parameter sets per flow. Read-only.
  • docsIetfQosServiceFlowTable: all flows known to the device, with direction and whether each is the primary flow. Read-only.
  • docsIetfQosServiceFlowStatsTable: packet and octet counters, creation time, active seconds and policing counters.
  • docsIetfQosUpstreamStatsTable: fragmentation, discard and concatenation counts, measured at the CMTS upstream only.
  • docsIetfQosDynamicServiceStatsTable: counters for the dynamic service state machines.
  • docsIetfQosServiceFlowLogTable: a log of flows that no longer exist (CMTS only).
  • docsIetfQosServiceClassTable: named service classes, read-create on the CMTS and not implemented on a CM.
  • docsIetfQosServiceClassPolicyTable: maps external filter policies to a service class. Read-create on both CM and CMTS.
  • docsIetfQosPHSTable: payload header suppression rules. Read-only, and MUST be implemented on both CM and CMTS when PHS is supported.
  • docsIetfQosCmtsMacToSrvFlowTable: maps CM MAC addresses to the flow IDs that belong only to that CM. Downstream multicast flows are left out because they are not tied to one CM.

Packets are indexed per CATV MAC interface (ifIndex) and flow ID. The module also defines three textual conventions: an interface direction (downstream is 1, upstream is 2), a bit rate in bits per second counted from the Ethernet destination address through the frame check sequence, and a scheduling type for upstream flows.
sections.eli5: Eleven tables are like eleven notebooks. Most of them are for reading only, like a report card. A couple let the cable company write in named recipes for speed rules.

sections.title: Packet Classification and the ToS Field
sections.content:
The RFC explains why outside managers cannot create flow classifiers directly. Doing so would need coordinated classifier IDs and would expose service flow IDs, which the committee felt should stay internal to DOCSIS. What was wanted was to classify packets to a Service Class, not to a particular flow.

The solution reuses the existing IP packet filter table from RFC 2669. An outgoing packet is checked against that filter table, which yields a policy ID. The policy table points to a row of this MIB's service class policy table, which supplies a Service Class Name and a rule priority. The MAC layer picks an active flow of that class (arbitrarily if there is more than one), then the packet class table may pick a different flow. If the two disagree, the greater of the two priorities decides. A packet that matches no policy goes straight to the packet class table.

By convention, internal classifier priorities should be in the range 64-191. External priorities in 192-255 override internal classification, and those in 0-63 are overridden by it. The mechanism applies both upstream from the CM and downstream from the CMTS.

The RFC also covers the IPv4 Type-of-Service octet. The ToS objects in the packet class and parameter set tables are read-only, while the service class table has a read-create DSCP overwrite object. This lets operators mark Differentiated Services values while preventing changes to the ECN bits.
sections.eli5: Imagine a mail room with a rule sheet saying letters from this person go in the fast lane. If the room's own sorter disagrees, whichever rule has the bigger priority number wins.

sections.title: Counters, Policing and Billing Logs
sections.content:
Packets are first classified to a flow, then policed against that flow's maximum rate by being dropped or delayed. The packet class counter counts every match regardless of what happens next. The flow table counts packets dropped by policing, packets delayed but still forwarded, and total packets forwarded beyond the policing step. Drops that happen later, such as a transmit queue overflow, do not change these per-flow counters.

The dynamic service statistics table gives 14 counters in each direction per MAC interface. Eight count the DSx message types, and six count successful and failed additions, changes and deletions. All failure reasons are grouped into one count, so deeper troubleshooting needs vendor-specific tools.

The service flow log is meant to be polled periodically by traffic monitoring and billing agents. It records total packets and octets, creation and deletion times, active seconds and, for unicast flows, the CM MAC address for billing reference. How many records to keep and for how long is vendor-specific, and a control object lets a monitoring application delete records it has already read.
sections.eli5: The counters are like a scoreboard that tracks how many cars got through, how many were turned away and how many had to wait, and the log is a receipt book for lanes that have closed.

sections.title: Working Alongside DOCSIS 1.0
sections.content:
A device that supports DOCSIS 1.0 as well as 1.1 or 2.0 implements both the older tables of RFC 2670 and the tables of this MIB. The interoperation goal is that before registration the DOCSIS 1.0 MIB applies, and afterward either that MIB or this one applies, depending on the mode in which the modem registered.

The rules include that a CM and CMTS MUST NOT create rows in the parameter set or service flow tables until the modem registers as DOCSIS 1.1 or 2.0. When it does, any pre-registration QoS profile row used only by that modem MUST be removed, and the modem's service flows from its configuration file appear in this MIB. DOCSIS 1.0 modems do not have entries in this MIB at all.
sections.eli5: Old modems keep using the old rulebook, and newer modems switch to the new one when they sign up.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Some readable objects in the module may be sensitive. Unauthorized SNMP GET access to the classifier and PHS tables can reveal IP addresses permitted enhanced QoS, such as those in voice-over-IP sessions. The parameter set table can reveal Service Class Names that could be named in an unauthorized configuration file to obtain better service. The flow table can show when a call is in progress, and the statistics, log and MAC-to-flow tables can reveal the volume and direction of any flow.

The RFC says SNMP versions before SNMPv3 did not include adequate security. It RECOMMENDS the SNMPv3 security features, including its cryptographic authentication and privacy, and says deploying versions before SNMPv3 is NOT RECOMMENDED. Operators remain responsible for making sure only legitimate principals can GET or SET these objects.
sections.eli5: The meters could tell a snoop who is on a phone call and how much they use the internet. So only trusted people should be allowed to look, and the connection should be locked.
